“I agree. That's the best way. Shall we just join hands and swear we'll—”

“Oh, no, that ain't enough for this. That's all right for ordinary little trifles—especially with girls, because they'll turn on you anyhow and tell everything when they get mad—but something this big ought to be written down. And in blood.”

Tom approved the notion with his whole soul. It was solemn, dark, and terrible; the hour, their circumstances, and everything around them suited it. Finding a clean pine shingle in the moonlight, he drew a small piece of “red keel” from his pocket, turned his work towards the moon, and laboriously scratched out these words. With each slow downward stroke he caught his tongue tightly between his teeth, relaxing it whenever the stroke went upward.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears to keep quiet about This and wishes They may Fall dead right where They stand if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry marvelled at Tom's ease with writing and the grandeur of his expressions. He promptly pulled a pin from his lapel and prepared to prick himself, but Tom said:

“Wait! Don't do that. A pin's made of brass. There might be verdigrease on it.”

“What's verdigrease?”

“Poison, that's what. Just swallow a little once and you'll find out.”

Tom therefore stripped the thread from one of his needles, and both boys pricked the fleshy part of a thumb and pressed out a drop of blood. After a good deal of squeezing, Tom at last succeeded in writing his initials with the tip of his little finger for a pen. He then taught Huckleberry to form an H and an F, completing the oath. With gloomy rites and incantations they buried the shingle beside the wall, and regarded the chains upon their tongues as locked fast, with the key cast away.

Just then a figure slipped noiselessly through a gap at the far end of the ruined building, but neither boy observed it.

“Tom,” Huckleberry whispered, “does this mean we can't ever tell—not ever?”

“Of course. No matter what happens, we've got to stay mum. We'd fall down dead—don't you know?”

“Yes, I suppose that's right.”

For a little while longer they went on whispering. Suddenly a dog gave a long, mournful howl just outside, not ten feet away. The boys seized one another in a paroxysm of terror.

“Which one of us does he mean?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don't know—look through the crack. Quick!”

“No, you look, Tom!”

“I can't—I can't do it, Huck!”

“I might just as reasonably ask,” she replied, “why, with such an obvious intention of offending and insulting me, you chose to say that you liked me against your will, against your judgment, and even against your own character. Didn't that give me some excuse for discourtesy, if I was discourteous? But I have other grievances. You know I do. Even if my feelings hadn't already decided against you—if I had been indifferent, or even favorably inclined—do you imagine anything could induce me to accept a man responsible for destroying, perhaps forever, the happiness of a sister I dearly love?”

As she said this, Mr. Darcy's color changed, but the reaction was brief. He listened without trying to interrupt as she continued:

“I have every possible reason to think badly of you. No motive can excuse the injustice and lack of generosity you showed there. You dare not, and cannot, deny that you were chiefly, if not solely, responsible for separating them: for exposing one to public criticism for fickleness and inconsistency, the other to ridicule for disappointed hopes, and both to the most acute suffering.”

She paused, seeing with considerable indignation that his manner showed no trace of remorse. He even watched her with a smile of feigned disbelief.

“Can you deny that you did it?” she demanded again.

With an appearance of composure, he replied, “I have no intention of denying that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am delighted to have succeeded. I have been kinder to him than to myself.”

Elizabeth would not lower herself to acknowledge this courteous observation, but its significance was not lost on her, and it was hardly likely to make her more sympathetic.

“But this affair is not the sole basis of my dislike,” she went on. “My opinion of you was settled long before it happened. Your character was revealed in the account Mr. Wickham gave me many months ago. What can you possibly say on that subject? What imaginary act of friendship will you offer in your defense? What distortion of the truth will you use to deceive others?”

“You take a passionate interest in that gentleman's affairs,” said Darcy, his tone less composed and his color rising.

“Who could know his misfortunes and help taking an interest in him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated contemptuously. “Yes, his misfortunes have certainly been great.”

“And inflicted by you!” Elizabeth exclaimed with force. “You have reduced him to his present poverty—relative poverty.

At the sight of it, the Ourang-Outang leapt straight through the chamber door, bounded downstairs, and escaped into the street through a window which, unhappily, stood open.

The Frenchman pursued it in despair. Still grasping the razor, the ape would pause now and then, looking back and making gestures at its pursuer until he had almost reached it, and would then take flight once more. Thus the pursuit went on for a considerable time. The streets were utterly silent, for it was close upon three in the morning. As they passed along an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the escaping creature noticed a light shining through the open window of Madame L'Espanaye's room on the fourth floor of her house. It darted towards the building, discovered the lightning rod, and climbed it with astonishing nimbleness. Seizing the shutter, which lay thrown back flat against the wall, it used this to swing directly onto the bed's headboard. The entire performance took less than a minute. As it entered, the Ourang-Outang kicked the shutter open once again.

Meanwhile, the sailor felt both encouraged and troubled. He now strongly hoped to recover the animal, since it could hardly leave the trap into which it had entered except by the rod, where he could catch it upon its descent. Yet he had ample reason to fear what it might do inside the house. This anxiety drove him to continue after the fugitive. A lightning rod offers little difficulty to a climber, particularly a sailor; but once he had reached the height of the window, which stood well to his left, he could proceed no farther. All he could manage was to stretch sideways far enough to catch a view into the room. At what he saw, sheer horror nearly made him lose his grasp. At this moment those dreadful screams broke upon the night which roused the residents of the Rue Morgue from sleep. Madame L'Espanaye and her daughter, both in their nightclothes, had apparently been arranging papers in the iron chest previously described, which had been rolled into the centre of the room. It stood open, with its contents on the floor beside it. The unfortunate women must have been seated with their backs to the window; and the interval between the animal's entrance and their cries suggests that they did not discover it at once. They would naturally have supposed the shutter's closing to be caused by the wind.

When the sailor peered inside, the enormous beast had caught Madame L'Espanaye by her hair, which hung loose because she had been combing it, and was waving the razor about her face in imitation of a barber's movements.
